identification.summary: IronHusky is a Kaspersky-named, Chinese-speaking espionage actor that Kaspersky says has operated since at least 2017 [S1][S5]. Kaspersky linked it to the MysterySnail remote access trojan (RAT) in 2021, when MysterySnail was found alongside the Windows zero-day CVE-2021-40449 [S2][S3]. In 2025 Kaspersky reported a new MysterySnail version against government organizations in Mongolia and Russia [S1][S5].
identification.firstObserved: At least 2017 per Kaspersky [S1][S5]. CSO reports that older China-based infrastructure reused by MysterySnail goes back to 2012 [S3].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name is mapped in this record. No alias is stated in the sources gathered. Secondary coverage gives different start dates (2012 versus 2017), which come from separate claims: 2017 is the group's activity and 2012 is reused C2 infrastructure [S3][S7].

attribution.confidence: Kaspersky describes IronHusky as a Chinese-speaking threat actor [S1][S5]. Kaspersky tied MysterySnail to IronHusky because early variants showed code and functionality overlap with IronHusky-attributed malware and reused C2 addresses of the Chinese-speaking actor dating back to 2012 [S3][S7]. This is a vendor assessment; no government attribution or state sponsor was found.
attribution.basis: Malware code overlap and reused C2 infrastructure reported by Kaspersky [S3][S7].

objectives: Kaspersky-derived coverage describes the activity as espionage against IT companies, defense contractors, diplomatic entities and government organizations [S3][S5][S7].

sectors: Aviation and research institutes (per the imported record, not independently confirmed)
targeting.notes: The 2021 MysterySnail activity hit IT companies, defense contractors and diplomatic entities [S3][S7]. In 2025 the targets were government organizations in Mongolia and Russia [S1][S5]. Only Windows Server systems were observed attacked with the 2021 exploit [S7].

capabilities.summary: The 2021 intrusions used an elevation-of-privilege exploit for CVE-2021-40449, a use-after-free in the Win32k driver, fixed by Microsoft on 12 October 2021; it was deployed against Windows servers in late August and early September 2021 [S7]. The payload was the MysterySnail RAT, which collects system information and contacts a C2 server for further commands [S7]. The 2025 version is delivered through a malicious MMC script disguised as a document from Mongolia's National Land Agency (ALAMGAC); the script downloads a ZIP second stage and a decoy DOCX, and sets persistence through registry changes [S5]. The updated RAT supports almost 40 commands, and a lighter variant, MysteryMonoSnail, supports 13 commands and uses WebSocket for C2 [S5][S6]. C2 uses public file storage and the piping-server project [S5]. Earlier reporting says the group used common Chinese-speaking tools such as PlugX and PoisonIvy [S3].

campaigns.name: MysterySnail and CVE-2021-40449 zero-day
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky detected Win32k privilege-escalation exploitation on Windows servers in late August and early September 2021, deploying MysterySnail against IT companies, defense contractors and diplomatic entities. Microsoft patched the flaw on 2021-10-12.

campaigns.name: New MysterySnail version against Mongolia and Russia
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reported attempted deployments of a new MysterySnail version via a malicious MMC script posing as an ALAMGAC document, plus the lighter MysteryMonoSnail variant, against government organizations in Mongolia and Russia.

diamond.adversary: Chinese-speaking espionage actor tracked by Kaspersky as IronHusky; no state sponsor stated [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: MysterySnail RAT and MysteryMonoSnail variant, CVE-2021-40449 Win32k exploit, malicious MMC script delivery, PlugX and PoisonIvy in earlier activity [S3][S5][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 addresses reused from older Chinese-speaking activity dating to 2012; public file storage and piping-server project in 2025; WebSocket C2 for MysteryMonoSnail [S3][S5][S7].
diamond.victim: Government, military/defense contractor, IT and diplomatic entities in Mongolia and Russia [S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Not assessed; the only basis (a 2018 Mongolian IMF-timing report) could not be verified and was removed.
diamond.technology: Windows Server systems exposed to Win32k privilege escalation in 2021; Windows endpoints opening MMC scripts disguised as official documents in 2025 [S5][S7].

gaps: No state sponsor, tasking organization or government attribution found in the sources gathered.

The original Kaspersky/Securelist articles (2021 and 2025) could not be opened (fetch failed); details come from search-result summaries and secondary coverage and should be verified against the primary text.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Windows Server hosts at IT firms, defense contractors and diplomatic entities, and government endpoints that open official-looking documents, are the exposed terrain [S5][S7]. STEP 2: The actor has persisted across at least 2017 to 2025 with rebuilt tooling after reporting, so expect re-tooling rather than disappearance [S1][S5]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is zero-day or script-based delivery, then MysterySnail RAT with public-service C2 [S5][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against Mongolian and Russian government targets. MDCOA is use of a new privilege-escalation zero-day against Windows servers of defense or IT suppliers. Candidate indicators: unexpected MMC (.msc) script execution from downloads, new registry persistence keys, outbound connections to public file-storage services or piping-server hosts, and WebSocket C2 from servers [S5][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Kaspersky and Microsoft reporting on Win32k and similar server privilege-escalation flaws; patch timelines matter because the 2021 exploit preceded the patch [S7]. (2) Authorities: this record shows no US-specific victims, so relevance is as a partner-region and supplier-risk indicator; confirm reporting and sharing authorities before any action. (3) Mission assurance: harden Windows Server and restrict MMC script execution for document-style lures [S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with contractor and partner networks through established DIB channels.
